title: What Does Her Future Hold?
author: Elizabeth Helfant
summary: In this guest essay, the first installment of Nick Potkalitsky's Historical Present series, Elizabeth Helfant, Associate Head for Academic Affairs at Ravenscroft School, reflects on four years of working with AI in schools while holding her newborn granddaughter. She traces a handful of moments: a department chair certain that AI could not write well, a student wrongly accused of using AI who wanted to be taught rather than policed, and the arrival of agents that can log in and complete a student's coursework. These lead to her central question, which is not whether AI can do the work but whether schools have been built so that the work is worth doing yourself. She also considers whether AI could finally force schools to pay down what Punya Mishra calls pedagogical debt. She ends with hope that teachers who know each child will remain, and that adults will learn to listen to each other.
points: The essay is a reflective series of moments from 2023 to 2026 rather than a how-to, showing how an educator's view of AI shifted over four years.
A student accused of using AI said that no one was teaching them about it, which led the author to conclude that schools offered suspicion instead of education.
Agentic AI that can log in and complete coursework challenges the assumption that students must at least be present for the work.
The author frames the real question as whether schools are places where the work is worth doing yourself, not whether AI can do it.
Punya Mishra's idea of pedagogical debt offers a hopeful reading in which AI forces schools to fix long-deferred problems with schedules, assessment and essays.
quotes: I am thinking about what will live inside it by the time she is old enough to hold one. What is her world going to be? The phone can’t tell me. Nobody can.
She is defending something real. Writing is thinking, and thinking can’t be outsourced. She is leaning into the human thing we have both long asserted.
The student is asking for what schools exist to provide, guidance through the world as it actually is, and we are offering suspicion instead of education.

Now the work can be done by something that is not the student, logged in as the student. The question was never really whether AI could do the work. It is whether we have built a school where the work is worth doing yourself.

We have had Mind Brain and Education research telling us we need to change- that our practices are not always consistent with what we know about learning but we choose to put off fixing it. AI has made that debt due.
What if AI isn’t the thing that breaks school, but the thing that finally makes us pay down the debt? A lever long enough to move what we couldn’t move ourselves.

What I hope stays recognizable is a teacher who knows her, who asks what she thinks and then waits for the answer. I hope someone teaches her about the machines instead of only warning her about them.
